# Optimized Versions of a Function {#appendix-o-optimized-versions-of-a-function}

This appendix was added in this edition, following a suggestion that
Dominique made to the original author: show several versions of the
same code, from the simplest to the fastest, and what each change buys.
The function is the one every program that handles text needs, the
length of a null-terminated string, which
[Chapter 6](06-reading-and-writing-simple-records.qmd#chapter-6-reading-and-writing-simple-records)
writes as `count_chars` and the C library calls `strlen`. Read
[Chapter 12](12-optimization.qmd#chapter-12-optimization) first.

The Four Versions {#the-four-versions}
-----------------

All four are in one file, built as a shared library, `libstrlen.so`
(see
[Chapter 8](08-sharing-functions-with-code-libraries.qmd#chapter-8-sharing-functions-with-code-libraries)),
so that Python can test and time them:

```{.gnuassembler .numberLines include=resource/asm/0AO-01-strlen.s}
```

-   **Version 1** is `count_chars`: a stack frame, an index in _%rcx_,
    and a loop of five instructions per byte, with two jumps.

-   **Version 2** removes what the function doesn\'t need. It calls no
    other function, so it doesn\'t need a stack frame. A pointer
    replaces the index, and the length is computed once, at the end.
    Moving the test to the end of the loop leaves three instructions and
    one jump per byte.

-   **Version 3** replaces the whole loop with one instruction,
    `repne scasb` (see
    [String Instructions](appendix-b-common-x86-instructions.qmd#string-instructions)).

-   **Version 4** changes the method instead of the instructions: it
    looks at 16 bytes at a time with SSE2. `pcmpeqb` compares the 16
    bytes of _%xmm1_ with the 16 zeros of _%xmm0_ at once, `pmovmskb`
    turns the 16 results into 16 bits of _%edx_, and `bsf` finds the
    first 1 among them. Its reads are always *aligned*: they start at a
    multiple of 16, so a read never crosses from one page of memory
    into the next one, which might not exist (Linux gives memory in
    pages of 4096 bytes, see
    [Chapter 9](09-intermediate-memory-topics.qmd#chapter-9.-intermediate-memory-topics)).
    That is why the first block can start before the string: the
    function shifts out the bits of the bytes that come before it.

Testing Them {#testing-them}
------------

A faster function that gives a wrong answer is worthless, and the fast
versions are the easiest to get wrong: version 4 has special cases for
the first block, for every position of the string inside a block, and
for a zero in the first or a later block. This Python program calls
the four versions with every length from 0 to 100 and some longer
ones, each starting at the 16 positions of a block, and compares them
with Python\'s own `len()`:

```{.python .numberLines include=resource/asm/0AO-02-strlen-test.py}
```

`test.bash` runs it every time the examples are tested:

```{.text check=appo-strlen-test}
errors: 0
```

Timing Them {#timing-them}
-----------

This program times each version, and the `strlen` of the C library, on
a string of one million bytes:

```{.python .numberLines include=resource/asm/0AO-03-strlen-time.py}
```

Times change from run to run and from processor to processor, so
these are the fastest and the slowest of five runs, in nanoseconds per
byte, measured in the container that builds this book on an Intel Core
i7-7820HK (from 2017):

| Version | ns per byte | Compared with version 1 |
|---------|-------------|-------------------------|
| 1. `count_chars` | 0.28--0.31 | 1 |
| 2. Fewer instructions | 0.33--0.35 | A little slower |
| 3. `repne scasb` | 0.52--0.54 | About 1.8 times slower |
| 4. SSE2, 16 bytes at a time | 0.029--0.034 | About 9 times faster |
| C library | 0.016--0.018 | About 17 times faster |

What the Numbers Say {#what-the-numbers-say}
--------------------

-   **Fewer instructions are not always faster.** Version 2 runs three
    instructions per byte instead of five, and on this processor it is
    a little *slower*. Both loops handle one byte per iteration, and the
    processor already runs the instructions of an iteration in parallel
    (see
    [Appendix N](appendix-n-the-fetch-execute-cycle.qmd#what-a-modern-processor-really-does)),
    so removing some of them doesn\'t help, and the way a particular
    processor feeds a small loop decides the rest. Another processor may
    rank them the other way. That is why you measure instead of
    guessing.

-   **One instruction is not one step.** `repne scasb` looks like the
    shortest program, but the processor runs it as a loop of its own,
    which on most current processors is slow. String instructions are
    fast for copying and filling big blocks (`rep movsb`, `rep stosb`),
    not for searching.

-   **The big gain comes from the method.** Version 4 is about 9 times
    faster because it handles 16 bytes per iteration instead of one. No
    rearranging of the byte-at-a-time loop can get close.

-   **The library is faster still.** The C library\'s `strlen` checks
    which instructions the processor has when the program starts (with
    `cpuid`, see
    [Other Instructions](appendix-b-common-x86-instructions.qmd#other-instructions))
    and uses the widest ones, here AVX2, 32 bytes at a time, with more
    tricks than fit in this appendix. Use the library\'s functions unless
    you have measured a reason not to.

Exercises {#exercises-o}
---------

-   Version 4 always starts with an aligned block. Write a version that
    reads 16 bytes with `movdqu` (which doesn\'t need alignment) from
    the start of the string. Why can it crash when the string ends
    near the end of a page? (The C library reads unaligned too, but
    first checks whether the read would reach the next page:
    `objdump -d` of its `strlen` shows `and $0xfff` and
    `cmp $0xfe0` before the first read.)

-   Change version 2 to read 8 bytes at a time into a register and find
    a zero byte among them. (Search for \"determine if a word has a zero
    byte\" for the classic trick with `0x0101010101010101` and
    `0x8080808080808080`.) Add it to the test before timing it.

-   Run `0AO-03-strlen-time.py` on your computer. Do the versions rank
    the same way?
